screens.title: Capstone Project: Development & Iteration
screens.subtitle: From plan to working app—iterate, test, debug, and polish your MVP

narration.text: This chapter is where your capstone becomes a functioning app through repeated cycles of development, testing, and refinement. You will adopt small, time-boxed development cycles—sprints—so that large features become manageable tasks you can complete, verify, and demo. You will also learn practices that keep code readable and modular so features can be tested and changed without breaking unrelated functionality. Testing is treated as part of development: unit tests for isolated logic, integration tests for component interactions, and UI tests to validate the user experience. When bugs appear, you will use debuggers and logging to find the cause, and you will apply performance checks to keep the UI responsive and battery friendly. Finally, we cover how to gather feedback from beta users, prioritize fixes, and prepare a clear narrative for your final presentation. A simple example you will practice: implement a small feature such as adding and removing a list item, write a unit or widget test for it, and iterate based on test and beta feedback. Think of this chapter as the practical loop that turns design and architecture into a stable, presentable product—what will you polish first for your MVP?

keyIdea.title: What matters most
keyIdea.text: Iterate in small cycles, keep code modular so it's testable, and make testing and debugging part of everyday development.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll practice and demonstrate by the end of this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to plan and run short development cycles that produce verifiable progress, implement core features using modular code patterns so they are testable, and write tests at multiple levels to catch regressions early. You will also gain hands-on debugging skills and learn how to monitor and improve performance so the app feels responsive on mobile devices. Each objective connects to a practical milestone: a working feature, passing tests, and a stable demo. For example, you will split 'user authentication' into small tasks like UI, integration with an auth provider, and state handling, then write unit tests for state updates and an integration test for login flow. This objective-based approach helps you prioritize the most impactful work for your final demonstration and teaches you to surface and fix problems early. Keep in mind a common misconception: writing tests slows you down. In practice, tests prevent rework and make your later iterations faster and safer. Which objective will you prioritize first in your capstone sprint?

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Skills & Deliverables
screens.subtitle: Concrete competencies you will demonstrate with your capstone

narration.text: These objectives map to deliverables you can show: a working core feature, automated tests that pass, and a short demo script that explains your architecture and choices. You will demonstrate an ability to decompose an MVP feature into tasks that fit into sprints, implement those tasks with clean, modular code suited to your chosen framework, and write tests that protect behavior as you iterate. For example, implementing an item-add feature means splitting UI, state management, and persistence tasks, then writing a unit test for the state update and an integration test for persistence. You will also practice using breakpoints and strategic logging to trace bugs, and run basic performance checks such as measuring frame drops or excessive memory. A frequent misconception is that tests only benefit large teams; in fact, tests save time for solo developers by preventing regressions during refactors. By the end, you should be ready to present your feature, explain how it is tested, and respond to questions about trade-offs and future improvements.

screens.title: Adopt Agile Sprints for the Capstone
screens.subtitle: Turn large features into short, verifiable tasks

narration.text: Agile development gives you a practical rhythm: short sprints that produce working, testable increments. In your capstone, view each sprint as a commitment to deliver a vertical slice of functionality: user interface, business logic, and persistence working together. Start by decomposing each MVP feature into small tasks. For example, instead of implementing 'User Authentication' as one big job, create tasks like 'Design Login UI', 'Integrate Authentication Provider', 'Implement Login State', and 'Add Logout Flow'. This decomposition reduces risk and creates natural checkpoints for tests and demos. Use acceptance criteria for each task: describe the expected behavior and how you will verify it with a unit or integration test. A common misconception is to keep tasks focused on UI only; that often leaves business logic untested and fragile. Always include at least one code or test task per feature. In practice you should finish each sprint with a passing test or a working demo. This habit prevents last-minute integration problems and makes your presentation credible. Which small vertical slice will you complete in your next sprint? Adopt Agile Sprints for the Capstone means break features into vertical slices that include ui, logic, and tests so each sprint delivers verifiable progress.. In practical terms, turn large features into short, verifiable tasks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Sprint tip
keyIdea.text: Break features into vertical slices that include UI, logic, and tests so each sprint delivers verifiable progress.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Sprint Planning
Sprint Process (Example)
  1. Define the vertical slice. Choose a feature scope that includes UI, logic, and storage.
  2. Break into tasks. Create small tasks such as UI layout, API integration, state handling, and tests.
  3. Estimate and commit. Keep each task small so it fits within the sprint timebox.
  4. Implement & test. Write the feature and its unit or integration test before finishing the task.
  5. Demo & gather feedback. Run a short demo and log feedback for the next sprint.
Concrete example
Implement item add: UI input, state update in ViewModel, persist to local storage, and write a unit test for the state update.
Common mistake
Splitting tasks only by UI screens without including logic or tests leads to fragile, untested features.
Task Board Example
To Do
Design Login UI, Create ViewModel, Add persistence interface
In Progress
Implement state handling, write unit test for state update
Done
Login UI wired to ViewModel with passing unit test
Key Takeaway

Design sprints so each deliverable is testable and demoable; this reduces late integration work.

screens.title: Clean Code & Modular Design
screens.subtitle: Separate UI, business logic, and data access for maintainability and testability

narration.text: Clean code and modular design are practices that make your capstone maintainable and easier to test. Clean code emphasizes readability: meaningful names, small focused functions, and predictable control flow. Modular design means separating concerns into distinct layers or components — typically UI, business logic (ViewModel, Bloc, controller), and data access (repositories or services). This separation lets you test business logic without rendering UI, and swap implementation details without changing other layers. For example, implement a ViewModel that exposes state and methods to load and mutate it, while the UI subscribes to state changes. The UI then only handles rendering and user events. A common misconception is that modularity is extra work for small projects; in truth, even a small capstone benefits because modular code makes feature changes and debugging faster. Another practical benefit: testing becomes straightforward because you can inject mocks for data access and assert the ViewModel behavior in isolation. As you design modules, prefer explicit interfaces, small public methods, and limit shared mutable state. Consider: can you write a unit test for this logic without touching the UI?

keyIdea.title: Design principle
keyIdea.text: Separate responsibilities so each module is independently testable and easier to maintain.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Modular Design
Three-layer architecture
UI, Business Logic, and Data Access aligned so responsibilities do not overlap.
UI Layer
Renders views and forwards user events to the business layer. Keep it free of heavy logic.
Business Logic
Encapsulate state and behavior in ViewModels, Bloc, or controllers. This is the primary target for unit testing.
Data Access
Repositories and services handle persistence and network calls. Inject them so you can replace them with mocks in tests.
Concrete scenario
A ViewModel exposes an items list and addItem(); the repository persists items. The UI only calls addItem and observes items updates.
Pitfall
Putting network or DB logic in UI components makes testing and refactoring much harder.
Practical checklist
  • Can you test business logic without rendering views?
  • Are dependencies injected so you can replace them in tests?
  • Are functions small and named for intent?
Key Takeaway

Modular separation reduces coupling and makes your capstone easier to test, debug, and evolve.

screens.title: ViewModel Pattern (Kotlin) — Example
screens.subtitle: A simple ViewModel that loads and mutates state for the UI

narration.text: This example demonstrates a small, modular ViewModel that holds state and exposes methods to update it. The ViewModel isolates business logic from the UI and is straightforward to test. The loadItems method simulates asynchronous loading and updates LiveData when data arrives; addItem mutates state in a controlled way. In a unit test you can call these methods and assert the LiveData values without rendering UI. A common misconception is that state containers must be complex; in many cases a small ViewModel with clear public methods and private mutable state is both sufficient and preferable. When testing, avoid relying on real network delays—inject a repository that returns deterministic data or use a test coroutine dispatcher to control timing. This ViewModel pattern maps well to Android, iOS MVVM analogs, Flutter providers, and React Native state containers: keep logic in a layer you can instantiate and call from tests. Consider: can you test addItem when the repository fails? That edge case should be part of your test plan. ViewModel Pattern (Kotlin) — Example means put state and state-change methods in a viewmodel so you can assert behavior in unit tests without ui dependencies.. In practical terms, a simple viewmodel that loads and mutates state for the ui. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Testable logic
keyIdea.text: Put state and state-change methods in a ViewModel so you can assert behavior in unit tests without UI dependencies.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › ViewModel Example
Kotlin ViewModel (read-only example)
<!-- Kotlin code example -->
class MyViewModel : ViewModel() {
  private val _items = MutableLiveData<List<String>>()
  val items: LiveData<List<String>> get() = _items

  fun loadItems() {
    viewModelScope.launch {
      delay(1000) // Simulate network delay
      _items.value = listOf("Task 1", "Task 2", "Task 3")
    }
  }

  fun addItem(item: String) {
    val currentList = _items.value.orEmpty().toMutableList()
    currentList.add(item)
    _items.value = currentList
  }
}
This pattern isolates state and provides clear methods that are easy to unit test by asserting LiveData values after calling methods.
Walkthrough & test guidance
  • loadItems() uses a coroutine scope and updates LiveData when data arrives; in tests, use a test dispatcher or mock repository.
  • addItem() mutates a copy of the current list and posts a new value—this makes state changes observable and testable.
  • Test idea: call addItem and assert the new list contains the added element and has expected size.
Analogy
Think of the ViewModel as a small controller that owns the app's current state snapshot and provides actions to change it; the UI is a passive observer of that state.
Key Takeaway

Keep logic in a testable class and avoid placing business rules inside UI components.

screens.title: Testing: Unit, Integration, and UI Tests
screens.subtitle: A multi-layered approach that catches errors early and validates user flows

narration.text: Testing should be an integral part of your capstone workflow. The testing pyramid is a useful model: many fast unit tests at the bottom, fewer integration tests in the middle, and a small number of end-to-end or UI tests at the top. Unit tests verify individual functions or classes in isolation and are fast to run frequently. Integration tests check how components work together, for example a ViewModel interacting with a repository. UI or instrumentation tests simulate user interactions to ensure screens behave as expected, but they are slower and more brittle. For a capstone, aim to write unit tests for business logic first—these will catch logic errors during rapid iteration. Then add a few integration tests for important flows like login or adding items, and a single UI test that verifies a critical path. A common misconception is to rely only on manual testing; manual checks miss regressions and slow development. Instead, add tests incrementally as you implement features. Practical example: when you implement addItem, add a unit test asserting that the ViewModel list increases, and an integration test ensuring the repository persisted the item. Which behavior will you protect with a unit test first?

keyIdea.title: Testing pyramid
keyIdea.text: Favor many unit tests, some integration tests, and a few UI tests to balance speed and coverage.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Testing Strategy
Testing Pyramid
Unit Tests
Fast tests for individual functions and classes; run them often during development.
Integration Tests
Verify that modules work together correctly, for example ViewModel and repository interactions.
UI / Instrumentation Tests
Simulate user flows to validate user experience; use sparingly for critical paths.
Practical checklist
  • Write unit tests for business logic first.
  • Add integration tests for flows that combine modules.
  • Create one or two UI tests for the app's critical path.
Example
Unit test: assert addItem increases list length. Integration test: ensure item persisted via repository. UI test: simulate add flow and observe new item in list.
Key Takeaway

Balance test speed and coverage: fast unit tests prevent many regressions; use broader tests for integration and UI confidence.

screens.title: Write a Simple Widget Test (Flutter) — Example
screens.subtitle: A small widget test that verifies UI behavior and state changes

narration.text: This coding example shows a compact widget test that verifies a counter increments when a button is tapped. Widget tests run in a simulated environment and check UI behavior without launching a full device emulator. The test builds the widget tree, asserts initial state, simulates a tap, and then asserts the changed state. This is ideal for your capstone when you want to validate a user interaction such as adding an item or toggling a setting. A common misconception is that widget tests are the same as manual QA; widget tests are automated and repeatable, but they can be more brittle if the UI structure changes frequently. To reduce brittleness, assert visible outcomes—like the displayed text—rather than internal widget hierarchies. For your capstone, start by writing a widget test for one critical interaction, run it in CI or locally during development, and add more tests as features stabilize. Which interaction in your app would benefit most from a widget-level assertion? Write a Simple Widget Test (Flutter) — Example means widget tests simulate user interactions and assert visible outcomes so you can catch regressions early.. In practical terms, a small widget test that verifies ui behavior and state changes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Test the UI
keyIdea.text: Widget tests simulate user interactions and assert visible outcomes so you can catch regressions early.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Widget Test Example
Flutter widget test (counter example)
// Example widget test
import 'package:flutter_test/flutter_test.dart';
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';

void main() {
  testWidgets('Counter increments smoke test', (WidgetTester tester) async {
    await tester.pumpWidget(const MyApp());

    expect(find.text('0'), findsOneWidget);
    expect(find.text('1'), findsNothing);

    await tester.tap(find.byIcon(Icons.add));
    await tester.pump();

    expect(find.text('0'), findsNothing);
    expect(find.text('1'), findsOneWidget);
  });
}
Tip: make assertions on visible text and behavior rather than on internal widget structure to keep tests robust.
Test checklist
  • Build the widget in the test harness.
  • Verify initial state with expect() calls.
  • Simulate user actions with tester.tap() and tester.pump().
  • Assert final state matches expectations.
Common mistake
Relying on timing without controlling pumps can make tests flaky; prefer deterministic pumps and mock async sources.
Key Takeaway

Automate critical UI interactions with widget tests to prevent regressions and speed iteration.

screens.title: Debugging Fundamentals and IDE Techniques
screens.subtitle: Use breakpoints, stepping, and variable inspection to find and fix bugs efficiently

narration.text: When bugs appear, a systematic approach turns confusion into progress. Start by forming a reproducible scenario: what user action leads to the error, what device state is required, and whether it is intermittent or consistent. Use your IDE’s debugger to set a breakpoint where you suspect the issue originates, then step into the code to observe function calls and variable values. Modern debuggers let you inspect object state, evaluate expressions, and change variables at runtime — use those abilities to test hypotheses without changing source files. A concrete example is stepping through a ViewModel load function while simulating a slow network; observe how cached values and state transitions occur and where nulls or unexpected values appear. A common misconception is that logging alone is sufficient; logs are valuable but stepping through a live debugger reveals control flow and variable lifetimes that logs cannot. Equally important is pruning the search space: isolate the failing module with unit tests or a minimal reproduction so you can iterate quickly. Practice using conditional breakpoints to pause only when specific conditions occur and watch expressions to track values over time. Finish each debugging session by writing a small test or adding a defensive check so the same regression cannot easily return. What small test could you add now to prevent this bug from reappearing?

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: Use reproducible steps, live debugging, and targeted tests to find root causes faster than relying on logs alone.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Debugging Fundamentals
Why live debugging matters
Observe runtime state and control flow to confirm hypotheses and locate root causes.
Checklist
  • Reproduce the bug reliably or create a minimal test case.
  • Set conditional breakpoints to target the failing path.
  • Inspect variables, step into functions, and evaluate expressions.
  • Record a short failing unit test once the issue is isolated.
Key Takeaway

Live debugging reveals program flow and state in ways logs cannot; pair it with small tests to prevent regressions.

Step-through example
A minimal ViewModel load function that you can step into from your IDE. Use a breakpoint on the network call to watch state transitions.
class MyViewModel : ViewModel() {
  private val _items = MutableLiveData>()
  val items: LiveData> get() = _items

  fun loadItems() {
    viewModelScope.launch {
      // breakpoint: inspect 'result'
      val result = repository.fetchItems() // simulate network or DB
      _items.value = result
    }
  }
}
Common Mistake
Relying only on logs and guessing control flow leads to long fix cycles. Use stepping to verify assumptions.
Pro Tip
Add a small unit test after fixing the bug to lock in the expected behavior and speed future refactors.
Try this
Open your IDE, reproduce a bug, set a conditional breakpoint, and step through the failing method. When you understand the cause, add a focused unit test that reproduces the bug and then asserts the correct outcome.

screens.title: Strategic Logging and Network Inspection
screens.subtitle: Use logs, structured messages, and network inspection to understand runtime behavior

narration.text: Logging and network inspection are complementary observability tools. Structured logs record events and context over time, while network inspectors show request and response payloads and timing. Start by choosing a minimal, consistent logging format: a short tag for the area (for example, auth or sync), a clear message, and any contextual fields such as user ID, request ID, or latency. This makes searching and filtering in IDE log windows or centralized log dashboards much faster. For network troubles, reproduce the failure and capture the request with a proxy or the platform’s built-in network inspector. Look for incorrect URLs, wrong HTTP methods, missing headers, or error status codes. An example workflow: add a log before a network call, inspect the actual HTTP exchange with a proxy to verify payload and headers, then add a post-response log with status and parsed result. Beware of a common misconception: more logs do not always help. Excessive logging can obscure the useful messages and slow down performance, so log at appropriate levels (debug vs info vs error) and remove or lower verbosity in release builds. Finally, redact sensitive fields and use conditional logging for heavy loops. Which two fields would you include in every network log to make triage faster?

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: Combine concise structured logs with network captures to pinpoint API and integration issues quickly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Logging & Network Inspection
Logging pattern
Use a concise tag, a single action phrase, and contextual fields to make logs searchable and actionable.
Recommended fields
  • Request or correlation ID to link traces end-to-end.
  • Short tag (module or feature) and severity level.
  • Timing information such as elapsed ms for network calls.
Privacy reminder
Never log PII or sensitive tokens. Mask or redact before sending logs to any server or developer console.
Example logs and network inspection
Log.d("auth", "login_request", mapOf("userId" to userId, "requestId" to requestId))
// After response
Log.d("auth", "login_response", mapOf("status" to response.code, "latencyMs" to elapsed))
Use a proxy or the platform inspector to capture the raw HTTP exchange. Look at request headers, body, and server responses to detect mismatches.
Common Mistake
Leaving debug-level logs in release builds can leak data and impact performance.
Pro Tip
Give each request a correlation ID and return it with error messages so you can match client logs with server logs quickly.
Try it

Add a short debug log around a failing network call and run a proxy to capture the HTTP payload. Verify headers and body match your expectations.

screens.title: Avoiding Main-Thread Blocking and Resource Hotspots
screens.subtitle: Move work off the UI thread, optimize images, and reduce unnecessary work

narration.text: Mobile users expect responsive apps. When the UI thread is blocked by long-running work, the app freezes or stutters, causing poor user experience. The central principle is: keep the main thread focused on rendering and input, and move heavy computation, file input and output, or network calls to background threads or asynchronous tasks. On Android, use coroutines or background executors; on iOS, use Grand Central Dispatch to move C P U or network work to a background queue. For Flutter and React Native, use async tasks or isolates when needed. A concrete example: charging a large image decode on a background thread prevents jank during scroll. Another common hotspot is repeated or synchronous database queries in a rendering loop — cache results or batch queries. Measure before you optimize: use profiler tools to find C P U, memory, or network bottlenecks rather than guessing. A typical misconception is premature optimization: changing code without data often wastes time. Instead, run a profile, identify the slowest frames or the highest allocation paths, and target those areas. Finally, remember power usage: frequent wakeups, excessive animations, and large network transfers hurt battery life. Optimize images, reduce redraws, and debounce rapid events. Which user action in your app is most likely to cause a long-running task on the main thread?

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: Profile first, then move slow or heavy work off the UI thread and reduce redundant work to keep the app responsive and efficient.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Performance Optimization
Performance first
Use profiling tools to identify slow frames, heavy allocations, and hotspot functions before changing code.
  • Move long tasks off the UI thread (coroutines, GCD, async/await, isolates).
  • Optimize images by resizing and using appropriate formats.
  • Batch or cache I/O and network calls to reduce work during rendering.
Comparison
Main-thread work: UI freezes and dropped frames. Background work: smooth interactions and responsive UI. Profile to decide where to move work.
Pro Tip

Use sampling profilers for CPU hotspots and memory allocation traces to find unexpected allocations that cause GC pauses.

Kotlin coroutine example: move work off main thread
fun loadAndProcess() {
  viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.IO) {
    val data = repository.fetchLargePayload()
    val processed = heavyProcessing(data)
    withContext(Dispatchers.Main) {
      _uiState.value = processed
    }
  }
}
Common Mistake
Running heavy synchronous loops during UI rendering or decoding full-size images on the main thread.
Measure
Only optimize code paths identified by profiling. Measure before and after each change to confirm improvement.
Try this
Run the profiler, identify one slow frame or allocation, and refactor that code to run asynchronously. Re-run and compare the frame times to confirm the improvement.

screens.title: Beta Testing, Feedback Prioritization, and Iteration
screens.subtitle: Collect actionable feedback, prioritize fixes, and iterate quickly toward a stable MVP

narration.text: Beta testing turns assumptions into evidence. Use TestFlight, Google Play’s internal or closed testing tracks, or an equivalent beta channel to get real user feedback before your final presentation. Design a short test plan for beta users: what flows to exercise, what devices and OS versions to target, and what feedback questions to ask. Capture both qualitative feedback (what users say) and quantitative signals (crash reports, performance metrics, session lengths). When feedback arrives, triage it by impact: critical crashes and data loss go first, then core feature failures, then UX improvements and minor polish. Use agile sprints to schedule small, focused fixes: a one-day fix for a crash, a two-day story to improve onboarding, and so on. A helpful technique is the quick triage board: label feedback as P0, P1, or P2 and assign an owner. Incorporate device logs and reproduction steps with each issue to speed fixes. Remember, not all feedback should be accepted; distinguish between a single user preference and a systemic problem that hurts many users. After implementing fixes, push another beta build and verify the changes with a short smoke test. For your final presentation, highlight how user feedback shaped your decisions — that shows evidence-based development and makes your project more credible. What one metric would you monitor during beta to decide if your app is ready for the final demo?

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: Prioritize beta reports by severity, fix critical issues first, and iterate in small sprints to demonstrate steady progress informed by real users.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Beta & Iteration
Beta plan essentials
Define target devices, critical flows to test, and clear feedback questions for participants.
Capture
Screenshots, reproduction steps, and device logs with each report.
Prioritize
Use severity labels P0/P1/P2 to triage what to fix first.
Iterate
Ship small sprint-sized fixes and re-run a smoke test in the beta track.
Triage board example
A simple board with three columns: P0 (crash, data loss), P1 (core feature broken), P2 (UX polish). Assign each card an owner, estimate a small sprint, and track verification steps.
P0
App crash when saving a profile. Repro steps + logs attached.
P1
Item list fails to refresh on add. Affects core flow.
P2
Button label unclear on small screens.
Key Takeaway

Beta feedback is evidence. Triage by impact, fix what breaks core experience, and iterate in focused sprints to steadily improve the product.

screens.title: Final Presentation, Documentation, and Deliverables
screens.subtitle: Prepare a clear narrative, screenshots, README, and demo script to showcase your capstone

narration.text: Your final presentation is the story of your project: what you built, why you made the choices you did, and how you solved problems along the way. Start by crafting a short demo script that highlights the core user flows that prove your app is functional — the create-read-update-delete cycle, a key network interaction, and any distinctive feature. Capture clean screenshots or a short recorded demo of these flows on a target device or emulator. For code delivery, include a clear README that explains how to run the project, its architecture, chosen technology, and any setup steps such as A P I keys or emulator configuration. Also include a short section on challenges and how you resolved them; this demonstrates problem-solving. Create a separate test evidence folder with screenshots of passing unit or widget tests and the IDE test runner output. A common misconception is that only code quality matters; presentation and reproducible run instructions are equally important because reviewers must run your app to validate your claims. Finally, prepare a brief Q&A list: be ready to explain key design choices, trade-offs you made, and one optimization you would do next if you had more time. This shows reflection and readiness to grow. What two slides would you include to convince an evaluator that your app is production-ready?

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: A concise demo, clear README, and test evidence turn working code into a persuasive capstone deliverable.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.5 › Presentation & Deliverables
Demo script checklist
  • One-sentence goal of the app and target user context.
  • Walkthrough of core flows that show CRUD operations and any integrations.
  • Show a failing case fixed by your code (e.g., bug you resolved) and the test that prevents regression.
  • End with a stretch-goal or next step to show thoughtfulness.
README minimum sections
  1. Project summary and chosen technology.
  2. Setup steps to run locally including emulator and environment variables.
  3. Testing instructions and where test artifacts live.
  4. Known limitations and future improvements.
Key Takeaway

Deliver runnable code, clear instructions, and evidence of testing so evaluators can reproduce your results and appreciate your engineering choices.

Test evidence
Include screenshots of passing unit or widget tests and a short note on what each test verifies. This speeds grading and shows discipline.

Presentation tips
Practice the demo until each step takes under two minutes. Anticipate two questions: why this design and how you measured success.
Deliverables
Source repo, README, test artifacts, screenshots, short demo video (optional), and a brief reflection document describing challenges and solutions.

These three practices together reduce guesswork, improve performance, and make your app more reliable.
